lines: THE VILLAIN DRAWN TO SELL TOYS

vis.prompt: Dramatic low-angle shot of a quiet 1960s comic colorist's inking desk: a desk lamp, ink bottles, pencils, and stacked comic books nearby, a 1968 calendar visible on the desk. No dialogue bubbles, no sound-effect text, no background action or explosions. On the open comic page sits a rough inked line-art outline of an enormous, hyper-muscular superhero figure mid-stride: massively wide shoulders, huge thick arms and legs, an imposingly bulky powerhouse build, bald head with simple masked eyes (no helmet, no hair detail), plain unmarked sleeveless bodysuit with no chest emblem, no cape, no armor, no gadgets, unfinished sketch style. A paintbrush is mid-stroke, actively painting flat gray color inside the figure's outline, gray paint splashes and drips around it, heavy black ink outlines, halftone-dot shadows, dramatic rim lighting, dynamic diagonal composition

segments.text: Marvel printed his very first comic in 1962, and the printers had to guess one flat color for his skin, since nobody had ever drawn this character before.
The problem was the cheap newsprint of the sixties. It couldn't hold a flat gray tone, so it printed a different shade on almost every single page.
Some copies came out pale blue, others almost brown.

vis.prompt: Overhead shot of three freshly printed 1960s comic book pages fanned out side by side on a print shop table, each showing the same panel of an enormous, hyper-muscular superhero figure (massively wide shoulders, huge thick arms and legs, imposingly bulky powerhouse build, bald head, simple mask, plain unmarked bodysuit, no cape) — but each copy accidentally printed a different flat color: one pale blue-gray, one dull muddy brown, one true gray. Comic-book ink style, heavy black outlines, halftone dots, dramatic overhead lighting, dynamic diagonal composition

segments.text: So for issue number two, the team switched him to green — a color the old presses could print the same way, every single time.

vis.prompt: Recolor only the gray paint on the superhero figure to vivid green instead. Keep everything else in the image identical: the same line art, pose, hand, brush, desk, ink bottles and composition. Do not change the figure's design, add any detail, or change anything except the paint color from gray to green.

segments.text: It wasn't a creative decision. It was a printing deadline nobody in the room actually planned around.
And that unplanned mistake became the version every fan, every toy, and every movie has used ever since — a color nobody originally wanted, now impossible to imagine him without.

vis.prompt: Dramatic angled shot of a comic book shop shelf. The most prominent, front-and-center comic cover, titled 'NEON AVENGER', stars an enormous, hyper-muscular green-skinned superhero figure wearing a plain navy-blue unmarked bodysuit (massively wide shoulders, huge thick arms and legs, imposingly bulky powerhouse build, bald head, simple mask, no cape) in a dynamic leaping pose over a rubble-strewn city skyline, issue number 2 printed on the cover. Do not use purple anywhere on the figure's costume. Surrounding it on the shelf are several other unrelated invented comic titles and covers. Bold heavy black ink outlines, halftone-dot shading, dramatic angled composition
